scenes.tts: The first film showed how rhythms and cues time responses. What happens when cue patterns change for years? Return to the same dial. The nearest dial still holds a cherry bud. This time, stack many years behind it.

scenes.visual: Reuse film one's COLOR MAP exactly: light and day length BLUE; temperature RED; inner rhythm GOLD; response GREEN. Fill the frame with the same year dial. Duplicate it into a receding stack labelled MANY YEARS while every dial keeps turning slowly.
scenes.narration: The first film showed how rhythms and cues time responses. What happens when cue patterns change for years? Return to the same dial. The nearest dial still holds a cherry bud. This time, stack many years behind it.

scenes.visual: Brief title over the moving stack: When Nature's Calendar Shifts. The nearest dial remains large and turning.

scenes.tts: Long-term change can come from natural events or from people. Wildfires and floods can happen naturally. People can cause pollution and habitat destruction. Change can alter population size, location, relationships, or timing. Here we will follow timing, using one group of cherry trees.
scenes.caption: Long-term change can come from natural events or from people. Wildfires and floods can happen naturally. People can cause pollution and habitat destruction. Change can alter population size, location, relationships, or timing. Here we will follow timing, using one group of cherry trees.
scenes.visual: Around the dial stack, briefly transform four GREEN icons in place: many dots to few, a range patch sliding, linked species separating, and a calendar marker shifting. Fade the first three and enlarge a cherry twig beside the timing marker.
scenes.narration: Long-term change can come from natural events or from people. Wildfires and floods can happen naturally. People can cause pollution and habitat destruction. Change can alter population size, location, relationships, or timing. Here we will follow timing, using one group of cherry trees.

scenes.tts: Suppose winter and early spring become warmer across many years. A tree that responds to warmth may bloom earlier. On each new dial, the red warmth band reaches the bud sooner. The green bloom marker slides earlier on this schematic dial.
scenes.caption: Suppose winter and early spring become warmer across many years. A tree that responds to warmth may bloom earlier. On each new dial, the red warmth band reaches the bud sooner. The green bloom marker slides earlier on this schematic dial.
scenes.visual: Mark this sequence SCHEMATIC. Across three stacked dials, slide the RED warmth band gradually earlier. Each time it reaches a bud, a GREEN bloom marker appears. Keep may bloom earlier on screen to preserve uncertainty.
scenes.narration: Suppose winter and early spring become warmer across many years. A tree that responds to warmth may bloom earlier. On each new dial, the red warmth band reaches the bud sooner. The green bloom marker slides earlier on this schematic dial.

scenes.tts: But warmth is not the only cue. Many buds need enough cold first. If winter becomes too warm, some may open late or unevenly. Warming does not force every response earlier. Different timing systems can give different results.
scenes.caption: But warmth is not the only cue. Many buds need enough cold first. If winter becomes too warm, some may open late or unevenly. Warming does not force every response earlier. Different timing systems can give different results.
scenes.visual: Add a BLUE cold checkpoint before the RED warmth band. On one schematic dial, both pass and blooms open together. On another, the blue sector is shorter; bloom icons appear later and spread out. Label the outcomes MAY OPEN LATE OR UNEVENLY.
scenes.narration: But warmth is not the only cue. Many buds need enough cold first. If winter becomes too warm, some may open late or unevenly. Warming does not force every response earlier. Different timing systems can give different results.

scenes.tts: Now predict. One spring has an unusually early bloom. Does that single year prove the long-term pattern moved? The rest of the record stays hidden. Hold your answer while one green point appears on an empty timeline.
scenes.caption: Now predict. One spring has an unusually early bloom. Does that single year prove the long-term pattern moved? The rest of the record stays hidden. Hold your answer while one green point appears on an empty timeline.
scenes.visual: Transform the dial into a horizontal timeline. Place one GREEN point far on the early side. Show the question ONE YEAR PROVES A SHIFT? A thin cursor pulses beside the lone point.
scenes.narration: Now predict. One spring has an unusually early bloom. Does that single year prove the long-term pattern moved? The rest of the record stays hidden. Hold your answer while one green point appears on an empty timeline.

scenes.visual: Hold the lone green point and the question. Let the cursor pulse slowly. Do not reveal yes or no.

scenes.tts: No. One year can differ for many reasons. A long-term claim needs repeated observations made with the same rule. Observers use a fixed rule for peak bloom. At the Tidal Basin, observers recorded peak bloom across nearly a century.
scenes.caption: No. One year can differ for many reasons. A long-term claim needs repeated observations made with the same rule. Observers use a fixed rule for peak bloom. At the Tidal Basin, observers recorded peak bloom across nearly a century.
scenes.visual: Multiply the lone point into a long row of yearly GREEN points. Above them, show the fixed observation rule 70% OPEN as an on-screen number, not narration. A simple Tidal Basin outline and repeated cherry-tree icon anchor the location.
scenes.narration: No. One year can differ for many reasons. A long-term claim needs repeated observations made with the same rule. Observers use a fixed rule for peak bloom. At the Tidal Basin, observers recorded peak bloom across nearly a century.

scenes.tts: The record uses day of year. A smaller day number means an earlier date. That direction can feel backward at first. Imagine the year as a ruler from winter toward summer. Moving left means blooming earlier.
scenes.caption: The record uses day of year. A smaller day number means an earlier date. That direction can feel backward at first. Imagine the year as a ruler from winter toward summer. Moving left means blooming earlier.
scenes.visual: Transform the timeline into a large January-to-December ruler. Put DAY 1 at the left and DEC 31 at the right without speaking them; do not show 365 as the last day, since a leap year has day 366. Slide a GREEN bloom marker left and label the motion EARLIER.
scenes.narration: The record uses day of year. A smaller day number means an earlier date. That direction can feel backward at first. Imagine the year as a ruler from winter toward summer. Moving left means blooming earlier.

scenes.tts: Scientists can group years and compare mean bloom days. The plotted means wiggle. The line never becomes a smooth staircase. Several groups are later than the group before. After the group with the latest mean, the means move earlier, though not in a steady line.
scenes.caption: Scientists can group years and compare mean bloom days. The plotted means wiggle. The line never becomes a smooth staircase. Several groups are later than the group before. After the group with the latest mean, the means move earlier, though not in a steady line.
scenes.visual: Compute and plot the ten decade-group means from the lesson table: 92.7, 96.8, 93.4, 96.8, 97.4, 95.5, 93.3, 90.9, 90.7, 91.7. Label axes DECADE GROUP and MEAN DAY. Reverse the vertical reading cue with EARLIER near smaller values. Draw points and connecting line from the exact values.
scenes.narration: Scientists can group years and compare mean bloom days. The plotted means wiggle. The line never becomes a smooth staircase. Several groups are later than the group before. After the group with the latest mean, the means move earlier, though not in a steady line.

scenes.tts: Compare two groups on screen. Subtract the smaller mean from the larger mean. The smaller mean marks the earlier bloom. The difference shown is evidence of shifted timing.
scenes.caption: Compare two groups on screen. Subtract the smaller mean from the larger mean. The smaller mean marks the earlier bloom. The difference shown is evidence of shifted timing.
scenes.visual: Highlight 1950–1959: 96.8 and 1990–1999: 90.9. Show 96.8 − 90.9 = 5.9 days entirely on screen. Do not highlight 1930–1939 or 2000–2009; students compute that pair in the lesson. Move a GREEN marker left by the computed difference. Keep the rest of the plot faint but visible.
scenes.narration: Compare two groups on screen. Subtract the smaller mean from the larger mean. The smaller mean marks the earlier bloom. The difference shown is evidence of shifted timing.

scenes.tts: Be careful with the claim. These trees in one city do not represent every species. The dates show a pattern, but they alone cannot prove what caused it. Testing cause needs temperature evidence too.
scenes.caption: Be careful with the claim. These trees in one city do not represent every species. The dates show a pattern, but they alone cannot prove what caused it. Testing cause needs temperature evidence too.
scenes.visual: Frame the plot with the label ONE GROUP OF TREES, ONE CITY. Keep the RED temperature band nearby but do not draw a causal arrow. Replace a tempting equals sign between temperature and bloom with a question mark labelled CAUSE NEEDS MORE EVIDENCE.
scenes.narration: Be careful with the claim. These trees in one city do not represent every species. The dates show a pattern, but they alone cannot prove what caused it. Testing cause needs temperature evidence too.

scenes.tts: The dial, record, and limit fit together. Organisms use timing systems. Long-term conditions can move the cues they meet. Responses may shift, while the details still depend on the organism. A careful claim keeps both pattern and limit.
scenes.caption: The dial, record, and limit fit together. Organisms use timing systems. Long-term conditions can move the cues they meet. Responses may shift, while the details still depend on the organism. A careful claim keeps both pattern and limit.
